This is the order, and He began with the hypocrites, saying: ﴿And they say, "We believe in Allah and the Messenger"﴾ with their tongues, ﴿and we obey﴾ Allah (p-513) and the Messenger. ﴿Then a party of them turns away after that﴾, i.e., it turns away from submitting to the judgment of Allah and His Messenger, ﴿after that﴾, i.e., after their saying ﴿"We believe in Allah and the Messenger and we obey"﴾. ﴿And those are not believers﴾, i.e., not the sincere ones. This refers to those who said "We believe and obey," not only to the party that turned away. In it is an announcement from Allah that belief is negated from all of them, because of their holding the beliefs that this party holds. And although the turning away may be from some of them, the approval of the turning away comes from all of them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 24, verse 48:

﴿And when they are called to Allah and His Messenger﴾, i.e., to the Messenger of Allah, like your saying: "Zayd's generosity amazed me," meaning the generosity of Zayd. ﴿So that he may judge between them﴾, the Messenger, ﴿when a party of them turn away﴾, i.e., a party among them suddenly turned away. It was revealed concerning Bishr, the hypocrite, and his Jewish opponent, when they disputed over a piece of land. The Jew kept dragging him to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), while the hypocrite was dragging him to Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, saying: "Muhammad is unjust toward us."

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿And if the right is theirs﴾ — that is, if the right belongs to them against others — ﴿they come to him﴾, to the Messenger, ﴿willingly submissive﴾ (muz'inin). This is a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: hastening in obedience, seeking their right, not out of contentment with the judgment of their Messenger.

Al-Zajjaj said: al-idh'an (submissiveness) is hastening together with obedience. The meaning is: because they know that with you there is only the bitter truth and the pure, unmixed justice, they refuse to be brought to judgment before you when the truth is against them, lest you snatch it from their very eyeballs by your ruling against them in favor of their opponents. But if a right is established for them against an opponent, they hasten to you and are content only with your judgment, so that you may take for them what is owed to them by the debtor (the opponent).

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 24, verse 50:

﴿Is there in their hearts a sickness, or have they doubted, or do they fear that Allah and His Messenger will be unjust toward them?﴾ He divided the matter regarding their turning away from his judgment when the right is upon them: that they are people of sick hearts, hypocrites; or that they doubt concerning the matter of his prophethood; or that they fear injustice (ḥayf) in his judgment. Then He nullified their fear of his injustice by His saying, ﴿Rather, it is they who are the wrongdoers.﴾ That is: they do not fear that He would be unjust toward them, because of their knowledge of his state (p-514), but rather they are wrongdoers who want to wrong the one to whom the right is due from them. And that is something they are not able to do in the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Therefore they refuse to be brought to judgment before him.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 24, verse 51:

﴿Only the saying of the believers﴾ And it is reported from al-Hasan that it was read as "qawlu" (in the nominative), but the accusative (qawla) is stronger, because the more definite of the two nouns is the better one to be the subject (ism) of kana (was), and "an yaqulu" (that they say) is more definite than "qawlu" (saying), unlike "qawlu al-mu'minin" (the saying of the believers). ﴿When they are called to Allah and His Messenger, that he may judge﴾ the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, that he may judge, i.e., that he may pass judgment ﴿between them﴾ by the judgment of Allah which was revealed to him, ﴿that they say﴾ "We hear" ﴿His saying﴾ "and we obey" ﴿His command﴾. ﴿And those are the successful﴾, the triumphant.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 24, verse 52:

﴿And whoever obeys Allah﴾ in His obligations (fara'id) ﴿and His Messenger﴾ in his sunnah ﴿and fears Allah﴾ regarding what has passed of his sins ﴿and is mindful of Him﴾ regarding what lies ahead ﴿those are the victorious﴾. It is related that one of the kings asked about a sufficient verse, and this verse was recited to him, and it comprises the causes of success. "Wa yattaqihi" (and is mindful of Him): Abu 'Amr and Abu Bakr read the ha' with sukun, intending pause (niyyat al-waqf); Hafs reads the ha' with a brief, weakened kasra (mukhtalasah); and the others read it with a kasra on the qaf and on the ha'.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 24, verse 53:

﴿And they swore by Allah with their most emphatic oaths﴾. That is: the hypocrites swore by Allah with the utmost of oaths, because they expended their utmost effort in them. "Jahd aymanihim" (the utmost of their oaths) is a metaphor borrowed from "jahida nafsahu" (he exerted himself), when one reaches the limit of its capacity. This is what happens when one goes to extremes in swearing and reaches the peak of its intensity and vehemence. It is related from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that whoever says "by Allah" has exerted his oath to the utmost. The underlying form of "aqsama jahd al-yamin" is "aqsama bi-jahd al-yamin jahdan," then the verb was deleted and the verbal noun (masdar) was placed first and put in its position, made genitive-annexed to the object, as in His saying: ﴿so strike the necks﴾ [Muhammad: 4]. The status of this accusative noun is the status of a circumstantial accusative (hal), as if he said: "striving with their oaths."

﴿If you were to order them, they would certainly go forth.﴾ That is: if Muhammad ordered us to go forth to the raid, we would certainly raid, or to leave our homes, we would certainly leave.

﴿Say: Do not swear;﴾ do not swear falsely, because that is disobedience.

﴿Known obedience﴾ is more fitting and more appropriate for you than these false oaths. It is a deleted subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, or the predicate of a deleted subject, meaning: what is demanded of you is known, recognized obedience, about which there is no doubt and no uncertainty, like the obedience of the sincere among the believers, not oaths you swear with your mouths while your hearts are contrary to them.

﴿Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾ He knows what is in your inner selves, and nothing of your secrets is hidden from Him, and He will surely expose you and requite you for your hypocrisy.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 24, verse 54:

﴿Say: Obey Allah and obey the Messenger.﴾ The shifting of the speech from the third person (absence, al-ghaybah) to the second person (address, al-khitab), by way of iltifat (the grammatical shift of address), is more forceful in rebuking them. ﴿But if they turn away, then upon him is only what he has been charged with, and upon you is what you have been charged with.﴾ He means: if you turn away, you have not harmed him; you have only harmed yourselves. The Messenger is only responsible for what Allah the Exalted charged him with and assigned to him, namely conveying the message. So when he has conveyed it, he has discharged his obligation. As for you, upon you is what you have been charged with, namely receiving it with acceptance and submission. If you do not do so and turn away, you have exposed yourselves to the wrath of Allah and His punishment. ﴿And if you obey him, you will be guided.﴾ That is: if you obey him in what he commands you and forbids you, then you have secured your share of guidance. Thus the harm of your turning away and the benefit both return to you. ﴿And upon the Messenger is only the clear conveyance.﴾ Upon the Messenger is only that he convey what has benefit for you if you accept it, and there is no harm upon him in your turning away. Al-balagh here means al-tabligh (conveying), just as al-ada' means al-ta'diyah (discharging). Al-mubin means the manifest, because it is accompanied by the signs and miracles. Then he mentioned the sincere ones (al-mukhlisin), saying:

﴿God has promised those of you who believe and do righteous deeds﴾. The address is to the Prophet ﷺ and to those with him. ﴿Of you﴾ (min-kum) is explanatory (li-l-bayan). It was also said that what is meant is the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun), and that min is partitive (li-l-tab'id). ﴿He will surely make them successors in the land﴾, that is, the land of the disbelievers. It was also said: the land of Madinah. The sound view is that it is general, based on the Prophet's ﷺ saying: "This religion will certainly reach everywhere that the night reaches." ﴿as He made successors those before them﴾. "Made successor" (istukhlifa) refers to Abu Bakr. ﴿And He will surely establish for them their religion which He has approved for them, and He will surely change [their state] for them﴾. "Wa-liyubaddilannahum" (with light tashdid) is read by Makki, and by Abu Bakr. ﴿after their fear, security﴾. God promised them that He would grant Islam victory over disbelief, give them the land as inheritance, and make them successors in it, as He did with the Children of Israel when He made them inherit Egypt and Syria after the destruction of the tyrants. [He promised] that He would distinguish the approved religion, which is the religion of Islam; its establishment (tamkin) means its confirmation and strengthening; that He would secure their path and remove from them the fear they were in. This is because the Messenger of God ﷺ and his Companions remained in Makkah for ten years in fear. When they emigrated, they were in Madinah, where they would rise in the morning and go to sleep at night armed, until a man said: "There will not come upon us a day when we are safe and can lay down our weapons." Then this verse was revealed, and the Prophet ﷺ said: "You will not wait long before a man among you sits in a great assembly, reclining, with no weapon with him." So God fulfilled His promise: He made them victorious over the Arabian Peninsula, they conquered the most distant lands of the East and the West, tore apart the kingdom of the Kisras (Persian kings), possessed their treasures, and took control of the world.

The oath implied by the lam and nun in "la-yastakhlifannahum" is omitted; its estimated sense is: God promised them and swore that He would surely make them successors. Or the promise of God, in its certainty, is treated as an oath, and is governed by what an oath is governed by, as if God had sworn: "God swears that He will surely make them successors."

﴿They worship Me﴾. If you take this as a resumptive clause (isti'naf), it has no grammatical position (la mahalla lahu), as if it was said: "What is their state that they are made successors and given security?" So He said: "They worship Me." If you take it as a circumstantial clause (hal) from "God has promised," meaning: God promised them that in the state of their worship, then it is in the accusative case (mahalluhu al-nasb). ﴿They do not associate anything with Me﴾. This is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the subject of "ya'budunani," meaning: they worship Me as monotheists. It is also permissible that it be a substitute circumstantial clause (hal badal) from the first circumstantial clause.

﴿And whoever disbelieves after that﴾, that is, after the promise. What is meant is ingratitude for the blessing, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and it disbelieved in the favors of God﴾ [al-Nahl: 112]. ﴿Those are the defiantly disobedient (al-fasiqun)﴾. They are the complete ones in their defiance, since they disbelieved this great blessing and dared to disregard it. It was said: the first to disbelieve this blessing were the killers of Uthman, may God be pleased with him. Then they fought each other after they had been brothers, and fear departed from them. The verse is the clearest evidence for the soundness of the caliphate of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, may God be pleased with them all, because those made successors who believed and did righteous deeds are them.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 24, verse 56:

﴿And establish the prayer﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf) with "obey Allah and obey the Messenger." The intervening separation does no harm, even though it is long. ﴿And give the zakah and obey the Messenger﴾ in what he calls you to. The obedience to the Messenger is repeated as an emphasis on its obligation. ﴿That you may be shown mercy﴾: that is, so that you may be shown mercy, for these are among the things that bring about mercy. Then he mentioned the disbelievers and said:

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 24, verse 57:

﴿Do not think that those who disbelieve can escape [Allah] within the earth.﴾ That is: they cannot escape Allah by being out of His power there. The tā' (in lā taḥsabanna) is an address to the Prophet ﷺ, and he is the subject (fā'il), and the two objects (maf'ūlān) are ﴿those who disbelieved﴾ and ﴿escaping﴾. With the yā' (as a reading), it is Shāmī and Ḥamzah, and the subject is the Prophet ﷺ because his mention has preceded, and the two objects are ﴿those who disbelieved﴾ and ﴿escapers﴾.

﴿And their refuge is the Fire.﴾ It is conjoined (ma'ṭūf) to "Do not think that those who disbelieve are escapers," as if it were said: those who disbelieve will not elude Allah, and their refuge is the Fire. ﴿And wretched is the destination.﴾ That is, the place of return (al-marji'), which is the Fire.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 24, verse 58:

﴿O you who have believed, let those whom your right hands possess ask permission of you﴾ is a command that the male and female slaves should ask permission. ﴿And those among you who have not reached puberty﴾, i.e., the children who have not yet reached puberty (ihtilam) among the free. It is also read with the letter lam pronounced with sukun (silent), for lightening (takhfif). ﴿Three times﴾ in the day and the night, and these are ﴿before the prayer of dawn﴾, because it is the time of rising from the beds and taking off the garments in which one sleeps and putting on the garments of wakefulness. ﴿And when you put off your clothes at midday﴾, which is the middle of the day in the heat of summer, because it is the time of putting off clothes for the midday rest (qaylulah). ﴿And after the prayer of the night﴾, because it is the time of stripping off the garments of wakefulness and wrapping oneself in the garments of sleep. ﴿Three times of privacy (awrat) for you﴾: that is, they are the times of three awrat, so the subject and the modifying noun have been omitted. The reading with the accusative (naṣb) is by Kufans other than Hafs, as an apposition (badal) of "three times", meaning: the times of three awrat. Each of these states has been called awrah because a person's concealment is disturbed in them, and awrah means a defect; from it comes a'war (one-eyed), the one whose eye is defective. A boy from the Ansar called Mudlij ibn Amr entered upon Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, at midday while he was sleeping and his garment had become uncovered from him. Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "I wish that Allah had forbidden entering at this hour except with permission." So he went to the Prophet ﷺ, and the verse had been revealed to him. Then He excused them for not asking permission outside these times by His saying: ﴿There is no blame on you or on them beyond these﴾, i.e., there is no sin on you or on those mentioned for entering without permission beyond these times. Then He explained the reason for not asking permission at these times by His saying: ﴿They are constant attendants upon you﴾, i.e., they go about with the needs of the household, ﴿some of you to others﴾: the subject (mubtada') whose predicate (khabar) is ﴿upon others﴾. Its estimated form is: some of you are going about upon others, so "going about" (ta'if) is omitted because "constant attendants" (tawwafun) indicates it. It is permissible that the sentence be a substitute (badal) for the one before it, and that it be an explanatory and emphasizing clause, meaning: you and they have a need for close association and mingling; they go about you for service, and you go about them for employment. So if the command to ask permission were absolute at every time, it would lead to hardship, and this is removed in the Shari'ah by the text. ﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you the verses﴾, i.e., just as He explained the ruling on asking permission, He makes clear to you other verses that you needed to have explained. ﴿And Allah is Knowing﴾ of the interests of His servants, ﴿Wise﴾ in explaining His intent.

﴿And when the children among you reach puberty﴾, meaning the free ones, not the slaves (*mamalik*), ﴿the age of ḥulum﴾, meaning *ihtilam* (reaching maturity through wet dreams). That is, when they reach that age and wish to enter upon you, ﴿let them ask permission﴾ at all times, ﴿as those before them asked permission﴾, meaning those who had reached the age of *ḥulum* before them, namely the men, or those mentioned before them in His words: ﴿O you who have believed, do not enter houses other than your houses until you have asked permission and greeted their occupants﴾ [al-Nur: 27], and so on. The meaning is that children are permitted to enter without seeking permission, except at the three times of privacy (*al-'awrat al-thalath*). When children become accustomed to this, and then reach maturity through *iḥtilam* or by age, they must be weaned from that habit and required to ask permission at all times, like the grown men who were not accustomed to entering upon you except with permission. People are heedless of this.

From Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them: three verses were denied by people, the permission altogether, and His words ﴿Indeed, the most honorable of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13], and ﴿And when relatives and orphans and the needy are present at the division﴾ [al-Nisa: 8]. From Sa'id ibn Jubayr: they say it is abrogated (*mansukha*, i.e., *naskh*, abrogation); by Allah, it is not abrogated. And His words ﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you His verses, and Allah is Knowing﴾ of the interests of mankind ﴿and Wise﴾ [al-Nur: 58] in what He has made clear of the rulings.

**﴿And the women past child-bearing﴾**, the plural of *qā'id* (قاعِد), because it is one of the descriptions specific to women, like *ṭāliq* (divorced) and *ḥā'iḍ* (menstruating). That is, they are women who have ceased from menstruation and childbearing because of their old age. **﴿Of the women﴾** is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). **﴿Who do not hope for marriage﴾**, meaning they have no desire for it. It is in the nominative position as a qualifier of the subject (*mubtada'*), which is *al-qawā'id*, and its predicate (*khabar*) follows. **﴿There is no blame upon them﴾**, meaning no sin. The *fā'* (ف) appears in **﴿fa-laysa﴾** because the subject contains, through the *alif* and *lām* (the definite article), a sense of conditional (*shart*). **﴿That they lay aside﴾** means "in that they lay aside" (*fī an yaḍa'na*). **﴿Their garments﴾**, that is, the outer garments, such as the *milḥafa* (wrap) and the *jilbāb* (cloak) worn over the *khimār* (head-covering). **﴿Without﴾** is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*). **﴿Displaying adornment﴾**, meaning not showing adornment. It means hidden adornment, such as the hair, the chest, the shin, and the like. That is, they do not intend by laying these garments aside to display themselves (*tabarruj*), but to lighten their burden. The real meaning of *tabarruj* (ostentatious display, تَبَرُّج) is the effort to reveal what must be concealed. **﴿And that they refrain﴾**, meaning they seek chastity by not laying aside the garments, so they remain covered. This is the subject (*mubtada'*), whose predicate (*khabar*) is **﴿better for them﴾**. **﴿And Allah is All-Hearing﴾** of what they declare, **﴿All-Knowing﴾** of what they intend.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 24, verse 61:

﴿There is no blame on the blind, nor is there blame on the lame, nor is there blame on the sick﴾. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib said: When the Muslims went out to the expedition (ghazwa) with the Prophet ﷺ, they would leave the keys of their houses with the blind, the sick, the lame, and their relatives, and they would permit them to eat from their houses. But they used to feel uneasy about this, saying, "We fear that their souls are not content with that." So the verse was revealed as a concession for them. ﴿Nor upon yourselves﴾, meaning: there is no blame ﴿that you eat from your houses﴾, meaning: the houses of your children, because a man's child is part of him and his ruling is the ruling of his own self. For this reason the children are not mentioned in the verse. The Prophet ﷺ said: "You and your property belong to your father." Or [it means] the houses of your spouses, because the spouses become like one soul, so the house of the woman is like the house of the husband. ﴿Or the houses of your fathers, or the houses of your mothers, or the houses of your brothers, or the houses of your sisters, or the houses of your paternal uncles, or the houses of your paternal aunts, or the houses of your maternal uncles, or the houses of your maternal aunts﴾, because permission from these is established by implication. ﴿Or what you possess the keys of﴾: "mafatih" is the plural of "miftah," which is that by which the lock is opened. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: It is the agent of a man and his steward over his estate and livestock; he may eat from the fruit of his estate and drink from the milk of his livestock. The meaning of possessing the keys is that they are in his hand and under his guard. It was also said that what is meant is the house of his slave, because the slave and what is in his hand belong to his master. ﴿Or your friend﴾, meaning: or the houses of your friends. "Sadiq" may be singular or plural, and it is the one who is sincere to you in his affection. A man from the early generations (salaf) would enter the house of his friend while he was absent, and he would ask his maidservant for his purse and take whatever he wished. When the master returned and she informed him, he would free her out of joy at that. As for now, stinginess has overcome people, so nothing is eaten except with permission. ﴿There is no blame upon you that you eat together﴾, gathered together, ﴿or separately﴾, dispersed, plural of "shatt." It was revealed concerning the Banu Layth ibn 'Amr, who used to feel uneasy about a man eating alone, so he would sometimes sit waiting all day until night; if he did not find anyone to eat with him, he would eat out of necessity. Or it was revealed concerning some of the Ansar: when a guest came to them, they would not eat except with their guest. Or they felt uneasy about gathering for food because people differ in how they eat and some exceed others. ﴿So when you enter houses﴾ of these houses in order to eat, ﴿then greet one another﴾, meaning: begin with the greeting upon its people, who are of your religion and kin, or [if] empty houses or a mosque, then say: "Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah." ﴿As a greeting﴾: it is in the accusative after "fasallimu," because it carries the meaning of "tasliman," like "I sat a sitting." ﴿From Allah﴾, meaning: established by His command and legislated from Him. Or because greeting and salutation are a request for safety and life for the one greeted, and life is from Allah. ﴿Blessed and good﴾: He described it with blessing and goodness, because it is a believer's supplication for a believer, from which increase in good and goodness of provision is hoped for from Allah. ﴿Thus Allah makes clear to you the verses, that you may understand﴾, so that you may reason or comprehend.

**Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 24, verse 62:**

﴿The believers are only those who have believed in Allah and His Messenger, and when they are with him upon a matter of common concern﴾, i.e., a matter for which people are gathered, such as jihad, planning in war, and every gathering for the sake of Allah, including the Friday prayer (al-Jumu'ah, the congregational Friday prayer) and the two Eids (the two festival prayers). ﴿they do not leave until they have asked his permission﴾, i.e., until he gives them permission. When Allah, Mighty and Majestic, willed to show them the magnitude of the offence in one leaving the gathering of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) without his permission, while they were with him upon a matter of common concern, He made their not leaving until they had asked his permission the third thing after belief in Allah and belief in His Messenger. He made these two like the prelude (al-tashbib, the opening lines before the main theme of a poem) and the groundwork (al-bisat, the foundation or preamble) for it. This was done by beginning the sentence with "only" (innama), placing "the believers" as the subject, and predicating of them a relative clause whose connection encompassed the mention of the two beliefs. Then He followed it with something that adds emphasis and intensity, when He restated it in another style, which is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who ask your permission, those are the ones who believe in Allah and His Messenger﴾. He also included something else within it, namely that He made seeking permission like the proof of the soundness of the two beliefs, and He alluded to the condition of the hypocrites and their slipping away furtively. ﴿So when they ask your permission﴾ to depart ﴿for some of their affairs﴾, i.e., their matters, ﴿give permission to whom you will of them﴾. In this is the elevation of his status, peace and blessings be upon him. ﴿And ask Allah's forgiveness for them; indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. The mention of seeking forgiveness for those who ask permission is evidence that the better course is not to ask permission. They said: it is fitting that people be likewise with their imams and their leaders in religion and knowledge, supporting them and not separating from them except with permission. It was said: it was revealed on the day of the Khandaq (the Trench, the Battle of the Trench). The hypocrites would return to their homes without seeking permission.

Commentary of al-Nasafi (Madarik al-Tanzil) on surah 24, verse 63:

﴿Do not make the summoning of the Messenger among yourselves like the summoning of some of you to others.﴾ That is: if the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has need of your gathering before him for a matter and summons you, then do not disperse from him except with his permission. And do not liken his summoning you to the summoning of some of you to others, or your leaving the assembly without the permission of the one who summons. Or [the meaning is]: do not make his naming and calling [of you] among yourselves like the way some of you name and call one another, by the name his parents gave him. Rather, do not say "O Muhammad," but say "O Prophet of Allah" or "O Messenger of Allah," with reverence, honour and a lowered voice.

﴿Allah already knows those among you who slip away﴾, going out little by little, ﴿furtively﴾. ﴿Liwadhan﴾ is a circumstantial state (hal), meaning: sneaking away one behind another. Al-liwadh (sheltering behind one another) and al-mulawadhah mean that this one shelters behind that one and that one behind this one, that is, they slip away from the congregation secretly, by way of mutual sheltering and some of them concealing themselves behind others.

﴿So let those who oppose his command beware﴾. That is, those who turn away from his command apart from the believers, and they are the hypocrites. It is said: "khalafahu ila al-amr" when one goes to the matter without him, and from this is the verse ﴿And I do not wish to go against you to what I forbid you﴾ [Hud: 88]. And "khalafahu 'an al-amr" when one turns away from it apart from him. The pronoun in "amrihi" refers either to Allah, glorified is He, or to the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace; the meaning is: [those who oppose] his obedience and his religion. The object of "yahdharu" is:

﴿that a trial should befall them﴾, a tribulation in this world, or killing, or earthquakes and terrors, or the imposition of an unjust ruler, or hardness of heart concerning the knowledge of the Lord, (p-523) or the lavishing of blessings as a gradual punishment, ﴿or that a painful punishment should befall them﴾ in the Hereafter. The verse indicates that the command here is for obligation.

Verse 64: "Surely to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth." The "alā" (ألا) here is an alert (tanbīh), calling attention to the fact that they should not oppose the command of the One to whom belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth. "He knows what you are upon" (قَدْ يَعْلَمُ ما أنْتُمْ عَلَيْهِ). The "qad" (قد) has been introduced to emphasize His knowledge of what they are upon of opposition to the religion, and the emphasis on knowledge returns to the emphasis on the threat. The meaning is: all that is in the heavens and the earth is exclusively His in creation, possession, and knowledge, so how could the conditions of the hypocrites be hidden from Him, even if they strive to conceal them? "And the Day they are returned to Him" (وَيَوْمَ يُرْجَعُونَ إلَيْهِ). It is read with a fatha on the yā' and a kasra on the jīm by Yaʿqūb (ويعقوب), meaning: He knows on the Day they are brought back to His recompense, and that is the Day of Resurrection. The address (khiṭāb) and third-person form (ghaybah) in His saying "He knows what you are upon and the Day they are returned to Him" may both be directed at the hypocrites by way of iltifāt (shift of address), or "what you are upon" may be general, while "they are returned" refers to the hypocrites. "Then He will inform them" (فَيُنَبِّئُهُمْ) on the Day of Resurrection "of what they did" (بِما عَمِلُوا), meaning what they concealed of their evil deeds, and He will recompense them their due recompense. "And Allah is Knowing of all things" (واللهُ بِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ عَلِيمٌ), so nothing hidden is concealed from Him.

It is narrated that Ibn ʿAbbās (رضي الله عنه) recited Surat al-Nur from the pulpit during the season (al-mawsim) and explained it in a manner that, had the Romans heard it, they would have embraced Islam. And Allah knows best.
